instructions: The night before, or at least 1 hour ahead: put the ribeye in the freezer for about 20 minutes to firm it up, then slice it as thin as you can against the grain.
In a bowl, grate half the Asian pear and mince the garlic and ginger. Whisk them together with 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1/2 cup brown sugar, the sesame oil, and the black pepper.
Add the sliced beef to the marinade, toss to coat, cover, and refrigerate overnight or for at least 1 hour.
The next day, rinse the rice and cook it according to the package so it's ready when the beef is.
While the rice cooks, julienne the carrots and slice the scallions, keeping a few sliced scallions aside for garnish.
Heat a cast iron or heavy skillet over high heat until it's just starting to smoke, then add the vegetable oil.

Add the beef in a single layer, working in two batches so the pan stays hot and the beef sears instead of steaming. Let it sit untouched for about 1 minute so it browns, then stir and cook another 1-2 minutes until just cooked through with no pink left. Transfer to a plate and repeat with the second batch.

Once both batches are done, return all the beef to the pan for 30 seconds to reheat, then pour in any marinade left in the bowl along with 2 tbsp water. Let it bubble for about 1 minute, scraping up any browned bits, until it coats the beef in a glossy sauce.
Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more brown sugar or a splash more soy sauce.
Scatter the reserved scallions and sesame seeds over the beef. Serve over the rice with the lettuce leaves and julienned carrots alongside for wrapping.
advance_prep_notes: Marinate the beef overnight (at least 1 hour, ideally the night before) for the best flavor
method_notes: Only one version was accessible (the other URLs in the request set weren't provided/openable). Damn Delicious's bulgogi: ribeye steak frozen ~30 minutes to firm it up, then sliced thin against the grain. Marinade is the classic sweet-soy base: soy sauce, sugar, sesame oil, garlic, ginger, and grated Asian pear (for sweetness/tenderizing), mixed with the sliced beef and refrigerated anywhere from a short marinate up to overnight for deeper flavor. Cooking is fast — the thin marinated slices are seared in a very hot pan (cast iron recommended) for just a couple of minutes total, since the thinness and tenderizing marinade mean it cooks almost instantly and shouldn't be overcrowded or overcooked. Served traditionally with rice, lettuce/perilla leaf wraps, and ssamjang dipping sauce, plus optional veggie toppings like carrots or scallions. No other versions were read, so no cross-recipe agreements or differences can be reported.
